title: Pizza With 3n Slices
statement:
A round pizza is cut into `3n` slices, and `slices` lists their sizes going clockwise around the pizza (so the last slice sits next to the first). Three people share it in rounds until nothing is left:

- You take any one of the slices still on the pizza.
- Alice then takes the remaining slice right next to yours going anti-clockwise.
- Bob then takes the remaining slice right next to yours going clockwise.

After a round the leftover slices close up into a smaller circle. Return the largest possible total size of the slices you take.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating the game tries every pick in every round, which explodes quickly. Look instead at which slices end up yours. Each round removes your slice together with its two current neighbours, so no two of your slices are ever side by side on the original circle. The reverse also holds: any `n` slices with no two neighbouring each other (counting the first and last as neighbours) can be collected in some order. So the task becomes: choose `n = slices.length / 3` non-adjacent slices on a circle with the largest total.

A circle is awkward for DP, but the first and last slice cannot both be chosen. Solve two straight lines, one without the last slice and one without the first, and keep the better result.

## Approach

1. Set `picks` to `slices.length / 3`.
2. `bestOnLine(from, to)` runs a DP over `slices[from..to]`. `dp[i][j]` is the best total from the first `i` slices of that line while taking at most `j` of them.
3. For slice `i` (size `size`): `skip` keeps `dp[i - 1][j]`; `take` adds `size` to `dp[i - 2][j - 1]`, because the slice just before it must stay free. Store the larger.
4. Return `dp[length][picks]`. Sizes are positive and a line of `3n - 1` slices always has room for `n` separated picks, so "at most" ends up as exactly `picks`.
5. Return the larger of `withoutLast` and `withoutFirst`.

## Example 1, step by step

`slices = [1,2,3,4,5,6]`, so `picks = 2`. `withoutLast` works on `[1,2,3,4,5]`; its best pair with a gap is 3 + 5 = 8. `withoutFirst` works on `[2,3,4,5,6]`; its best pair is 4 + 6 = 10. The answer is `max(8, 10) = 10`, matching taking slice 4 first and slice 6 next.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each line has about `3n` slices and `picks = n` counts.
- Space: O(n²) for `dp` (two rows would be enough).

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the wrap-around: `[10,1,1,1,1,10]` gives 20 on a straight line but only 11 on the circle.
- You take exactly `n` slices, not as many as a line allows; capping `j` at `picks` matters.
- Taking slice `i` must look back two rows (`dp[i - 2]`), not one.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `picks` | how many slices you get, `n` |
| `from`, `to` | the ends of the straight line being solved |
| `length` | number of slices on that line |
| `dp` | `dp[i][j]`: best total from the first `i` slices taking at most `j` |
| `size` | size of the `i`-th slice of the line |
| `skip`, `take` | totals when slice `i` is left or taken |
| `withoutLast`, `withoutFirst` | best totals of the two lines |
